items.body: “A sail to Puzzuoli, little trips by land, cheerful walks through the most wonderful regions in the world! Beneath the purest sky, the most treacherous soil; ruins of inconceivable opulence, oppressive and saddening; boiling waters, clefts exhaling sulphur, rocks of slag defying vegetable life, bare, forbidding tracts; and then, at last, on all sides the most luxuriant vegetation, seizing every spot and cranny possible, running over every lifeless object, edging the lakes and brooks, and nourishing a glorious wood of oak on the brink of an ancient crater!” J. W. von Goethe – Italian Journey, Naples, 1 March 1787 On Acherusia, Manuel Carbone turns his attention to the Phlegraean Fields, the vast volcanic caldera stretching across the western edge of the Bay of Naples. Shaped by successive eruptions over thousands of years, the area encompasses twenty-four craters and volcanic structures, many now submerged beneath the sea. Since antiquity it has been associated with fire, myth and transformation: the steaming fumaroles of Solfatara were believed by the Romans to mark the forge of Vulcan, while Lake Avernus and the surrounding landscape inspired the belief that this was an entrance to the underworld. Yet the Phlegraean Fields are not simply an archaeological or mythical site. They remain one of Europe’s most closely monitored volcanic regions, a place where geological instability, dense urban life and centuries of cultural memory coexist. Having grown up in the area, Carbone approaches this landscape neither as an outsider nor as a documentarian, but as someone tracing the intersections between personal memory, environmental change and everyday life. “Driven to and fro by nature and history,” as Goethe would put it—both collective and personal—Carbone gathers sounds and acoustic cues over several days of walking through Pozzuoli and the surrounding area. As the walk progresses through gradual shifts in sonic perspective, Acherusia unfolds as a sequence of interconnected vignettes. Birds and wind dominate the opening passages before gradually giving way to water, turbulent weather and eventually the sounds of urban life: distant voices, traffic, footsteps and the subtle traces of habitation, as “the living live on merrily.” Beneath these recordings, restrained drones and discreet electronic interventions evoke the region’s subterranean forces, at times recalling the hiss of fumaroles or the imperceptible movements of the caldera itself. Unlike many field-recording albums, Acherusia never fetishises the act of listening, nor does it mistake documentation for distance. The recordings retain a strong sense of the recordist’s physical presence while refusing to romanticise either nature or history. Carbone documents a landscape shaped equally by volcanic processes and human endurance, recording during a period of heightened seismic activity without ever turning the work into a disaster narrative, all set against a boundless view of land, sea and sky. Alas, just as one might wish to meditate—even if feeling quite unfit for it—the walk is over all too soon. Should one have failed to make any notes amidst all this giddy excitement, Manuel Carbone’s PDF, included with the download, will facilitate any future recollection by virtue of his careful selection of photo collages. (With thanks to Goethe.) To walk us through the making of the album, we reached out to Manuel Carbone for an interview conducted by email. Acherusia takes its name from the ancient lake associated with the entrance to the underworld, and the Phlegraean Fields themselves have long been linked to myths of descent, transformation and instability. How much did these historical and mythological layers influence your listening to the landscape, and how did you balance those narratives with the everyday realities of contemporary life in Pozzuoli and the surrounding area? Acherusia is a work mainly based on my personal memory of these places and yes, those layers are definitely relevant to the piece. As a child, visiting those areas, since some of my siblings lived there, I could sense a certain aura of mystery. Surely back then I was influenced by what I learned at school, the tales and myths associated with the Phlegraean Field, but it is something I still experience even nowadays when I go there. It’s a familiar feeling, something dear to me and that hasn’t changed throughout the years. Something I still perceive when I’m there or just when I think about those places. I made a conscious decision, when I went there specifically to collect sounds for the exhibition (and performance at Errant Sound, Berlin) to make those very personal feelings of reminiscence the core of the work. As for the title, Acherusia, I wanted it to be a relevant aspect of the piece, but not really central to it, not predominant. I didn’t want the listener to think that this is a work based solely or mainly on some mysterious, ancient, dark mythology. These volcanic lakes, their neighbouring inhospitable fields, were thought to be the entrance to the underworld and that was a fact, nothing really occult (in the modern meaning of the term) about it. It was the natural elements, the geological features at the basis of that belief. And you can somehow understand why, when you are there – I recently went back specifically to collect new sounds for an episode of framework:afield (for Framework Radio) curated by myself and I managed to look at the Lake Avernus from above, for the first time, from the top of Monte Nuovo and I could clearly see why they thought the lake was the entrance to the underworld. It is difficult to put into words, you really have to be there to experience certain “optical illusions” given by the stillness of the lake’s water – and surely the landscape was radically different back then, with fumaroles and steams more frequent, yet it’s very strong and beautiful to experience nowadays. People living there today, consciously or unconsciously, sense that mysterious aura, I believe. I don’t want to romanticise this aspect too much, but I think they have it in them. It shows, somehow. Mostly, what I admire in the local people, and that’s another strong aspect of my affection for these places, is their strength and resilience in living there, their sturdiness in staying in a place so unstable. However, this covers many social and political aspects that I did not want to touch in this work. Many of these elements I surely stand for, but out of respect to these people and their conditions, and out of my personal incapability and unpreparedness of talking about these aspects, I preferred not to cover them… But at least I wanted somehow to show this resilience, even without giving it any clear explanation. Photography & collage by Manuel Carbone The work exists simultaneously as a soundwalk, an installation, a live performance and now an extended listening piece. In the gallery, the recordings were accompanied by photographs and found objects collected on site, creating a dialogue between sound and material traces. What is gained—or perhaps lost—when Acherusia is experienced purely as sound, detached from those visual and physical elements? I wouldn’t speak in terms of gains and losses – I see this as different experiences. For the exhibition the pictures were printed in black and white, at a very low resolution, taped to rice paper and attached to resonant wooden panels where you could listen to excerpts of the soundwalks. And the guests could look at and touch the organic and non organic objects collected and displayed… The release from Falt Records comes with a digital booklet showing higher resolutions of the same photographs. The experience is different even more so if you listen only to the extended piece on streaming platforms – only audio and at lower quality. And obviously also the live rendition of the piece is different, the way it might be performed, how the listeners take in the meaning of the sounds is different, but nothing is really gained or lost I think. One of the most striking aspects of the album is the tension between geological time and human time. The Phlegraean Fields are shaped by slow volcanic processes, yet the work is filled with fleeting human presences: distant voices, traffic, footsteps and traces of habitation. Were you consciously trying to document a landscape in transition, or did the piece emerge more from personal memories and your own relationship to a place that is both familiar and precarious? Yes, I was consciously trying to capture the human presence in a landscape that is in constant transformation. I did not want it to be something like “nature taking over a landscape slowly being abandoned by humans”…. Or anything like that. Clearly, human presence is different now and that’s another aspect of the constant transformation of the area. I went there to record my soundwalks during a period of frequent seismic swarms. I didn’t experience any though, and that also affected the nature of the recordings. Local people were being careful, obviously preoccupied, concerned and alert. It wasn’t easy either to reach certain areas of the Phlegraean Fields as the public transportation was interrupted on several lines for safety reasons, I had to walk for kilometres, and most things were shut down, schools were closed… Streets were definitely quieter than usual but human presence was there. It is there. In the final piece, I had to be extra careful not to give the impression I was walking around some ghost towns or abandoned places. Nothing like that. Traffic, families in a park, children, people jogging along the banks of Lake Miseno and Avernus, the city center of Pozzuoli was definitely less lively than usual, but surely it was lived. Photography & collage by Manuel Carbone Your practice often engages with memory, hauntology and the transformation of field recordings through manipulation and collage. Acherusia, however, often feels remarkably restrained, allowing silence, wind, water and environmental sounds to speak for themselves. How did working on this project affect your understanding of field recording? Did spending time in a territory defined by uncertainty and constant subterranean movement change the way you think about listening, documentation and the role of sound as a witness to environmental change? It is true that it sounds restrained and that surely was my intention. I wanted to keep the final recordings as close as possible to the original sources, so the editing was minimal, I only made a collage in chronological order, from day one to day seven, of my daily walks. Some recordings, such as the ones made with a geophone, are left out and I use them only when I play live. I still applied some manipulation (effects and various sonifications) in some parts of the final edit, as an aesthetic choice and to evoke the feeling of memory drifting in and out because of a certain place, a certain sound and mood. Working on this piece it has definitely changed my approach to listening and collecting/documenting the places I walk. I now keep the editing to a minimum, I don’t care much anymore about the imperfections that most field recordists comprehensively try to avoid or edit out – I now consider these as an inevitable part of the documentation, a way to establish my physical presence in these recordings. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Where should one begin when approaching the second album by Premiata Forneria Marconi? Perhaps with its surreal cover art? Or with the track "Appena un Po'", which opens with a medieval feel, where the clavichord gives way to heavy rock and the melody itself stretches and warps; there are echoes of Gentle Giant, yet the band's own distinct personality is already clearly present. They possessed such a vast array of instruments that they were an orchestra unto themselves, displaying a strong identity and unique signature style as early as their second album. As with all great compositions, the sheer grandeur of the ideas can sometimes overshadow the performance itself, simply because there are so many concepts at play. Bringing these ideas to life relied heavily on Flavio Premoli's use of the Mellotron, Minimoog, and clavichord, alongside the violin and flute work of Mauro Pagani."Generale" dazzles with that atonal piano, joined by the full band, violin, and then heavily distorted guitar, creating the impression that they had it all, and indeed they did; the ideas are richly developed, with no mere hinting followed by a lack of depth. I notice great originality in the arrangements, which is another significant detail, specifically how they blend the dissonant violin with the rest of the instrumentation, seemingly cutting across the frenetic rhythm. "Per un Amico" reveals an acoustic side, featuring guitar followed by bass after an initial, very subtle piano section. "Il Banchetto" is a classic, not just for the band but for music in general, embracing both the singer-songwriter approach and a style deeply rooted in Italian tradition. Following the core structure comes an instrumental section rich with symphonic trappings that envelop, adorn, and enrich the piece, allowing it to be performed in either style. As the Minimoog and harps resound, the sky depicted on the album cover seems to come to life.When Flavio Premoli played the piano, you could sense classical, jazz, and rock sensibilities, much like Keith Emerson, with everything in his mind... flowing to his fingers and from there to the keyboard."Geranio" is an even finer, more elaborate, and unusual composition, more subtle, that gradually builds its concept, revealing it drop by drop. Once again, the piano takes center stage, accompanied by a wealth of melody and harmony. The interplay between atonal acoustic guitars and the entering piano bridges the sections: the most optimistic and luminous one... and the darker, more captivating one, that distinctly Italian, almost tragicomic vibe, like a Fellini scene with the paint running in the rain... a faded flower turned black and white... all enhanced by the violin and those deeply emotive piano notes.The great edifice that is Italian progressive rock would not be the same without Premiata Forneria Marconi, proof of which lies in the fact that their impact is just as palpable in their absence as it is in their presence.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Even within a band whose universe allowed ample room for experimentation and improvisation, one could still expect a clear sense of purpose and direction, however difficult that direction might be to follow. Following Damo Suzuki's departure, with guitarist Michael Karoli taking over vocal duties, a period of adjustment and sonic reinvention was to be expected before the band found its footing again. "Dizzy Dizzy" benefits from the effective use of the violin, but "Come sta, La Luna" remains merely a tribal-style attempt, blending Mediterranean tango and even flamenco elements, that falls short; Karoli himself admitted that he never sang the way he played guitar, whereas Damo would let himself go and sing like just another instrument.In "Splash," the electric violin sounds like a high-pitched saxophone, and when it hands off to the guitar and keyboard, they create an atmosphere that is both atmospheric and nocturnal. Here, the flamenco vibe returns, blending well with that almost free-jazz improvisation.Chain Reaction continues to flirt with reggae, blending African percussion and a touch of blues with psychedelia. However, while it sounds good, it didn't strike me as being as focused or having as clear a direction as previous albums; even when those earlier records were chaotic, you could still buy into the premise they presented. For me, that never quite happens here.Quantum Physics is highly interesting and attempts to capture the spirit of old-school alchemy, featuring pivotal contributions from Holger Czukay on bass, Jaki Liebezeit on percussion, and Irmin Schmidt on organ. It creates a minimalist atmosphere, blending electronic elements with a forward-looking post-rock sensibility that perfectly suits the album's nocturnal mood.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Caminhos De �gua by Kaatayra is a very interesting take on the black metal sound, with no distorted electric guitars and very atmospheric melodic arrangements over screamed vocals and blast beats. A one man project by Brazilian multi instrumentalist Caio Lemos, Kaatarya is one of his many creative outlets, with this one focusing alot more on the beautiful aspect of his music, with certain elements being influenced by faro, soundtrack music, Brazilian folk & ambient, but all within a black metal texture. Very unique in style, with great dynamic vocals throughout, the production is handled very well to flesh out the changing styles throughout. Overall it's one of the most unique black metal albums I've heard in a long time. I'd give this a mid to high 7 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Rio Sem Nome.

items.body: Review by rdtprog — Robert Reed was influenced by the band Renaissance while thinking on what style of music he wantedfor this one. It is evident in the music, which is a softer magenta style of prog with moreorchestra and fewer guitars. The concept is to present each track for 1 tarot card related todifferent important figures in the past. The songs are less in your face than some of their moreprogressive albums, but with a couple of listening sessions, I started to enjoy the beauty of themelodies. We have 6 long tracks with 4 interludes to give the listener a rest. The attention to thearrangements of this music is impressive, sounding like a little orchestra with the use of a bell(the trademark of Robert Reed), string arrangements, and recorded choir sound. The drums, which areplayed by Nick D'Virgilio, use the tabla in some places. � So, this new album has a lot of classicalinfluences, and with the voice of Christina, you can't help but think of the Renaissance. This CDcomes with a DVD. Right now I don't think you can have a physical release of the CD only, but theDVD offers not only the 5.1 mix of the album but also more bonus content. 4 tarot cards.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — With VDGG having disbanded for the first time in early 1972 -due to the band members' exhaustion from their emotionally demanding musical endeavors and the overwhelming financial problems stemming from their modest commercial success- Peter Hammill focused his energy and inexhaustible creative drive on his second solo album, "Chameleon in the Shadow of the Night" (1973). Accompanied by his former bandmates from the now-defunct group, Hammill immerses himself -as one would expect from him- in biting reflections and stark insights on life, with a voice that is at times furious, at other times expressively vulnerable, but always steadfast.Minimalist instrumentation, framed by a charmingly rudimentary production that lends the album a special authenticity, allows Hammill to delve into themes such as disillusionment and the grueling routine of touring in the acoustic and hypnotic "German Overalls"; the parting of personal paths in the also acoustic, though more peaceful, "Slender Threats," or the melancholic "Easy to Slip Away," with the evocative touch of the hazy Mellotron; as well as the acceptance that everything has a beginning and an end in the resigned "In the End," one of the album's best tracks, where Hugh Banton's emotive piano notes accompany Hammill's heart-wrenching voice.On the other hand, the band's influence is also very much present on the album -after all, the English musician and VDGG are practically synonymous- especially on the restless and understated "Rock and Role," and above all on the closing track "(In the) Black Room / The Tower," an excellent, epic, and theatrical mini-suite led by Hammill's visceral vocals, with peaks of tension and introspective lulls that feature David Jackson's signature wandering saxophones and spectral flutes, Banton's piano notes, and Guy Evans's percussive rolls. Had the British band not broken up, it surely would have found a place on one of their albums from that era.Very Good.4 stars

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 979"1984-96 Overture" is the second compilation album of Pendragon and was released in 1998. Between 1984 and 2001 the band released several and numerous compilations and EP's. It was usual for Pendragon to record many songs that never were released on any of their studio albums. They were only released on EP's and appeared on six EP's "Fly High Fall Far" released in 1984, "Red Shoes" released in 1987, "Saved By You" released in 1991, "Nostradamus" released in 1993, "Fallen Dreams And Angels" released in 1994 and "As Good As Gold" released in 1996. So, it was perfectly normal that Pendragon released several compilations with many of those songs that never appeared on their studio albums. So, some of them appeared on three compilations "The Rest Of Pendragon" released in 1991, "Once Upon A Time In England Volume 1" and "Once Upon A Time In England Volume 2", both released in 1999. However, Pendragon did something strange, which was the release of the same compilation three times with three different names. Thus we have "1984-96 Overture" of 1998, and "A Hist�ria" and "The Round Table (1985-1998)", both of 2001. It seems the band decided to release three compilation albums focused in three different markets. "1984-96 Overture" was to the US market, "A Hist�ria" was to the Latin American market and "The Round Table (1985-1998)" was to the European market."1984-96 Overture" has eight tracks. The first track "Midnight Running" was originally recorded on their EP "As Good As Gold". It's a typical wonderful symphonic Barrett's track with a hypnotic rhythm very effective, clocking at almost 8 minutes. It has nice background keys, mellow and gentle vocals, catchy melody, nice chorus and some great guitar work as well. It has also a pleasant rhythm from the bass and drums, which changes nicely for the chorus. This is another superb piece in the usual style of Pendragon. It's probably the best track on "As Good As Gold". The second track "Sister Bluebird" was originally recorded on their EP "Fallen Dreams And Angels". It's very melodic, a romantic progressive ballad, with some wonderful guitar performance and nice keyboard work, which soon became one of greatest songs on that EP. It has melodic and harmonic changes from the basic musical idea, with several guitar solos and keyboard hymns, where the true clarity of the music is never disturbed. The third track "Paintbox" was originally recorded on "The Masquerade Overture". It's an excellent track with a nice musical atmosphere, great melodies and a memorable chorus. It has good keyboard work and a superb guitar playing by Nick Barrett. This is a great symphonic track. The fourth track "Ghosts" was originally recorded on "The Window Of Life". It's an excellent track with a great piano opening by Nolan, with very subtle and constant changes of melody and tempo. The final result is a very good rock piece. It shows that Pendragon makes good compositions with emotional vocals and a nice choral work. The fifth track "The Voyager" was originally recorded on "The World". It's a kind of an epic ballad with great keyboards and beautiful acoustic guitar work that could create a harmonic and engaging colourful palette of sounds. The sixth track "Dark Summer's Day" was originally recorded on their EP "Fly High Fall Far". It's a mellow ballad with a great emotional guitar break at the end of the song. It's a song with a fine melody, slightly jazz and bossa nova rhythm, nice harmonies, good keyboard work and a magnificent guitar playing. The seventh track "Total Recall" was originally recorded on "Kowtow". It's a lengthy progressive emotional track with good guitar work and some beautiful piano work added by Clive Nolan. I like this song very much because it represents one of the best progressive moments on that album. The eighth and last track "The Black Night (Previously Unreleased)" was originally recorded on "The Jewel". It's a lengthy track surprisingly full of musical changes all over the track. This is an excellent track that gives perfectly well the glimpses of what would be the later Pendragon's music. Still, this is a slightly different version of the original version.Conclusion: As I wrote above, "1984-96 Overture" is one of the three equal compilation albums with three different names released by the group for three different markets and in different years. This was the first one and it was the compilation released to the US market. "1984-96 Overture" is a very well representative compilation from the group, at the time, because it includes one track per album from their first five studio albums. It also includes two tracks taken from two EP's from the band and an unreleased version of "The Black Night", which actually is very similar to the original one. So, at first sight, we can say this is an excellent compilation album from the band. However, I don't think this is really true. Despite it being well representative of their career until that time, I think it doesn't reflect totally the real quality of the band's music. It's true that several tracks are really good but I sincerely think that it could barely be associated with their best musical works. So, in spite of "1984-96 Overture" being a good compilation album from the group, I think it's more interesting for Pendragon's fans, but can hardly be recommended as an essential album. Besides, if you need a good compilation from the band from this period, I really recommend "The History 1984-2000".Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by alainPP — THE SAMURAI OF PROG (TSoP) delivers a frenetic, rhythmic blend of old and new, vintage sounds on GENESIS and YES, with Steve ever faithful to the violin. The story of the Seven Voyages of Sinbad from the Arabian Nights serves as the concept for these perilous adventures sailing between Greece, India, and Persia. The album features eight compositions by Beppe CROVELLA, Stefano VICARELLI, Octavio STAMPALIA, Alessandro Di BENEDETTI of INNER PROSPEKT, Rafael PACHA, Mimmo FERRI, Marco GRIECO, and the latest addition, Chris ENGELS."Guided by the Moon" opens with an orchestral intro, a festive, jazzy South American folk sound; Steve's vocals are followed by Beppe's melting keyboards with a vintage Mellotron. The flute and violin bring this dark yet captivating piece to life, like an endless wave crashing against the estuary. Toni adds his 12-string guitar, accentuating the symphonic effect; a seascape in the outro. "The Valley of Diamonds" begins as a cinematic adventure, then becomes symphonic, before flirting with Deep Purple thanks to Stefano's vintage organ. The sound flirts with Alan Parsons before evolving under Kimmo's martial pads; edgy, punchy, then jazzy rock with the frayed piano and colorful synth, warm, nostalgic."Mark the Stars" features Steph with his gravelly vocals, a masterful operatic vocalist reminiscent of Ayreon's work, with rich backing vocals. Octavio on keyboards provides a symphonic, elegiac intro for the neo-prog track with its distinctive keyboards, the vocals prominent throughout. "End of the Day" features Alessandro's keyboards and a return to Persia. Michael recounts this fourth symphonic stranding in a pleasant, unhurried stroll before letting the orchestral variation unfold on a warm solo by Roine. The symphonic section, with flute and piano, intensifies, with Genesis in the distance, The Samurai close at hand, and The Flower Kings between the two; an ethereal piano coda."Trapped by Old Age," with Rafael at the helm, evokes Mike Oldfield from the outset with his Scottish flute and ancient instruments?viola and zither?suggesting a medieval piece. A festive vintage folk meanders during this dense, colorful break, becoming somewhat scattered. "The Isle of Wonder," with Mimmo as master of the notes, is a somber piece, with Daniel's mournful vocals over an avant-garde RPI melody. The piano takes center stage, an oppressive jazzy air emerging from a delicate, Genesis-esque flute. Four well-orchestrated sections flow seamlessly into one another, some improvised, the vocals lacking substance given the musical textures, such as the exotic darbuka."The Last Shore," with Marco at the helm, features a melancholic piano and a vibrant, vigilant riff. Steve returns to amplify this epic crescendo with his magical violin, like the characters transforming into birds. The powerful and captivating, swirling fresco blends Genesis and Kansas on an airy, mysterious, grandiose melody, ideal for launching into the fruity guitar solo. The epic finale, reminiscent of Arena, takes off in all directions. "Sinbad the Sailor" concludes with Chris composing in his singular style of introspective and dynamic chiaroscuro, navigating between Genesis and Yes, undeniably. Chris also sings, revealing his compositional work inspired by the great masters. The guitar solo shines, Gilmour-esque, before returning to the raw vocals over the acoustic guitar. The best is here.Progressive rock of yesteryear, the kind that took its time, navigating the murky waters of classical, jazz, and symphonic music. A melodic album brimming with sumptuous breaks, but ultimately lacking a cohesive, unifying structure.

items.body: Review by Drmick1971 — What aligns me with the music of Karfagen or more particularly with Antony Kalugin is his music is a journey. Each and every album of his takes on a musical voyage. I've always said the music that grabs me, that touches me is the music that propels my mind on a trajectory to somewhere. With the release of the new Karfagen album "Omni II" just does that. This is a massive album with the full title being "Omni II Act 1: The Glass of Time" and has a running time of 67 minutes and 39 seconds. There is basically three long tracks, Omni Parts 4, 5 and 6. The previous parts are on the first "Omni" album. Parts 4, 5 and 6 are broken further into 4 or 5 tracks in each part.Not only is this rich in time it is rich in musical guests. I won't list every guest as that would take up most of my review. Max Velychko returns on guitars and also returning with her voice of prosperous power and delicacy is Mariya Panasenko on the song "Shadow Bound". Good also to see Oleg Prokhorov back into the fold on bass. Added to these returning stars are some big names in the Prog Rock world including Michel St. Pere (Mystery), John Hackett on flute, Roine and Michael Stolt (The Flower Kings), Rob Reed (Magenta, Cyan, Sanctuary) and Yogi Lang (RPWL).As the title suggests "Glass of Time" there is a theme of time, the journey of life, the adventure, the moments, the people we encounter in our lives. We travel roads of different textures, we travel uphill and downhill, we swim in rivers of calmness and rapids. Antony culminates all these elements, themes, instruments and musicians into one amazing and astonishing effort that lifts you, touches you and brings wonder and magic to our ears.I only gave the predecessor "Omni" four stars in my review. I must have known "Omni II" would surpass it as I'm giving this five stars. I am not taking anything away from the previous album, all in all they are both 5 stars together.Not only does the music deserve praise, so does the artwork. The cover gives that historical feel with class. Something you might expect from a J.R.R. Tolkien novel. Of course there is the high production values. The sound that Antony produces has always been of the highest quality. Every note, every instrument and every voice is crystal clear.This symphonic potpourri and puzzle is seamless when put together and flows like quicksilver. Antony blends the instruments in their right place, he envisages the talent of the musicians in their appropriate slot. He is the master in his element.So all of you that want to go on a musical journey it is here. It thrives and pulsates and each track is a new experience and adventure. Just like life.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — You feel like you're walking the streets the moment Lost Tribe's second album begins, not that it lacks sophistication, but rather that it is challenging, brash, and provocative. David Binney brought a background steeped in both free jazz and funk. It captures the essence of the 90s New York scene, featuring Fima Ephron on bass alongside the dual guitars of Adam Rogers and David Gilmore.If Walkabout served as the introduction, Whodunit plunges us into the polymodal rhythms characteristic of Steve Coleman & The Five Elements, a group Gilmore played with, while Ben Perowsky drums with punk-like energy and speed. It sounds complex... it sounds jazzy, and ultimately, it sounds progressive, as we shall see later on. The bottom line is that the scorching energy and enduring modernity keep the album alive; the music sounds as fresh as if it had been composed today.There is something epic about "It's Not What It Is"; while the guitar plays one section, the saxophone plays another, layering them in a way that ultimately imbues the track with a martial, heroic feel. Then comes the second part, featuring funk improvisation and virtuosic solos from both guitarists."Daze Of Ol'" features D.J. Nas Tee on turntables and vocals by Tracey Amos, with David Binney on flute and a syncopated, distinctive drum beat, a hip-hop element that fits perfectly with the spirit of the album."Room Of Life" brings out Binney's jazzier side, with the band backing his free improvisations, leading up to "Steel Orchards" and a Robert Fripp-esque guitar riff that is subsequently overlaid with a saxophone line, leaving the two playing simultaneously and exploring counterpoint.90s independent cinema, the rock music that permeated and merged with jazz, and influences from the past all converged to give Lost Tribe its distinctive sound, a phenomenon similar to that of Groove Collective, with whom they were, in fact, contemporaries. This is evident in La Fontaine's calm saxophone or the jazz-funk of "Second Story," which seem to evoke the paintings of Jean-Michel Basquiat or Wassily Kandinsky."Planet Rock" has a more experimental sound, constructed in an almost minimalist fashion from a single guitar chord and a saxophone note; it evokes jazz, as well as distorted alternative rock, a 90s fusion sound. Then, a new, avant-garde melody emerges, built upon a dual-guitar arrangement, marking one of the album's most ambitious and compositionally accomplished tracks."Fuzzy Logic" deserves to be a new standard, the kind that would get radio airplay in an ideal world, with the bass, sax, and drums breathing oxygen and energy into the track while simultaneously building a melody that stands as a new classic.Ⓗ is almost a blend of heavy metal, free jazz, and rock, a farewell track that reveals the second album as a snapshot of an era, capturing how people lived and felt in a specific place and time... and, like any old photograph, it remains relevant and finds new resonance.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — With their second album, Apophenian Bliss, the quartet raises the stakes and explores further sonic possibilities, employing polyrhythms and harmonies shared between keyboard and guitar; on the opening track, "Astrology," they build upon their earlier Mahavishnu and Tony Williams' Lifetime influences by adding elements of the Jeff Beck Group and 70s fusion.Post-rock is present, echoing the sensibility of Tortoise and This Immortal Coil, yet the dense, psychedelic progression evokes a 70s mysticism while sounding thoroughly contemporary. The violence and heaviness are counterbalanced by an electric piano that plays and leaps amidst the flames without getting burned, even though the music itself is truly blazing.The baritone guitar contributes its distinctive sound; while Apophenia continues to reveal compositional traces of mentor McLaughlin, the final result, driven by the quartet's performance, is refreshing. When the guitar solo arrives, accompanied by the bass, the music ventures into less explored territory; best of all, it is not merely aimless wandering, as a melody eventually emerges. Red Kite Flight demonstrates that, despite their instrumental prowess, when harmony and melody come into play, even amidst chaos, they bring out the best in themselves. More than ever, much like vintage recordings, the album conveys a sense of spontaneity and the feeling that the music could head in any direction, a notion confirmed by the track "Morrasol." It sounds almost as if a Rhodes, specifically Chick Corea on the Rhodes, had been added to Black Sabbath... cosmic, wild, and magically elastic and permeable.The notion, the concept, of Progressive Jazz remains alive and present here in Sleep Tight, featuring a subtle yet complex composition; without resorting to stridency, the music evokes images of neon constellations or an erupting volcano with cooling lava... all underpinned by classical influences."Feet Don't Fail Me Now" tries its hand at funk with the quartet's signature energy, ramping up to full speed, featuring those sustained high notes where, if the guitar were a vehicle, it would be taking tight corners without ever lifting its foot off the gas.

items.body: Attalie keeps her voice low and close to the microphone on “A Dare”, and the live session builds around it with guitar and keys through a wash of reverb, a soft bassline underneath, and a saxophone that arrives warm and late. The tempo walks and she holds the same unhurried register from the first line to the last. She wrote the song at the point where every box had been ticked and the fulfilment had gone missing: “Staying comfortable no longer felt enough“, she says, and the lyric weighs what a life closer to her calling would cost her. Born in Kinshasa, she has worked a seam of quiet storm, jazz and rumba since her 2018 debut EP Polluted. Second EP Sigh was produced by Tshepang Ramoba, drummer with South African band BLK JKS, and its lead single “Homeless” premiered through The FADER before picking up play on BBC Radio 1Xtra, KEXP, KCRW and NTS. “A Dare” is her third single since October 2025, after “Carry Me” and “Light”, with an EP in preparation. Watch the live session for “A Dare” HERE and stream the studio single following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Attalie – A Dare (Live) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.excerpt: Coniglio has made an album that honors the craft of earlier soundscape practice while carrying it into a private, contemporary meditation on cause, chance and presence. It is beautiful, grave, lucid, quietly overwhelming. items.body: Coniglio has made an album that honors the craft of earlier soundscape practice while carrying it into a private, contemporary meditation on cause, chance and presence. It is beautiful, grave, lucid, quietly overwhelming. Programmed with the patience of reception, performed with exact mercy 13/19/32 A Catalogue of Delays by Enrico Coniglio   13/19/32 A Catalogue Of Delays opens like a machine that has learned to breathe, a gentle engine of memory where every tone casts a future shadow and every future shadow returns carrying a new tint. Enrico Coniglio, Venetian guitarist, composer, sound artist and environmental recordist, has long treated sound as a way of reading place, weather, ruin, industry, water and human trace. Here he turns that long devotion toward time itself. The city that shaped him seems present in the work, purified of postcard temptation. Venice appears as method, as humidity inside the signal, as patience, as refraction, as a pulse moving across stone, canal light and electrical air. The title gives the key to the whole undertaking. Thirteen, nineteen and thirty two seconds, with the longer delay doubled, form the temporal grammar from which the album grows. The source is a classic lineage of guitar synthesis and delay craft: Roland tones, the revered TC Electronic 2290, Eventide treatments, the living afterglo​w of Robert Fripp’s Soundscapes. Coniglio approaches this inheritance with care and gratitude, turning a tradition of looping guitar into a personal philosophy of consequence. A played note becomes a promise. Its return carries the exactness of a diagram and the tenderness of a recollection. The delay line becomes a moral instrument: it teaches the listener that every gesture continues to act after its first appearance, that sound is action prolonged. Across nearly forty five minutes the album unfolds as one broad organism. It has short luminous portals at each end and a central body that expands in slow waves, gathering density, brightness, fatigue, splendor and ash colored calm. The field recordings placed near the opening of a couple of pieces do exactly what they should do in Coniglio’s world: they give the electronic material a climate. They bring air into the circuit. Then the guitar synthesizer rises, sometimes choral, sometimes reed like, sometimes close to the soft pressure of an organ heard through water. The tonal mass favors low and middle bands, where the music gains weight, while upper harmonics enter as silver powder. The result feels tactile, a music one almost reads through the fingertips. What fascinates is the way the album makes order sound unstable while preserving its secret arithmetic. Delay is usually sold as atmosphere, a halo around the note. Coniglio treats it as architecture in motion. The repeated events meet and fold into asynchronous constellations, precise in origin, sensuous in effect. The ear receives them as drift, and the system knows where each return belongs. This creates the record’s deeper emotional charge: a calm fatalism crossed by choice. The device predicts; the musician intervenes. A line is placed into the circuit, then life begins inside the pattern. Each new note changes the moral temperature of what came before. Each silence becomes an act of composition. The album carries drama through pressure, through the way a tone gathers companions until it resembles a weather front, through the way a harmonic shimmer slowly acquires a body and then yields to a darker current. Coniglio’s sound palette cultivates duration as an ethical practice. One senses a musician trained by field work, by the discipline of listening before naming, by the humility required to follow a place through its smaller signals. That background gives 13/19/32 a special gravity. In its purely synthetic passages, it feels observed, programmed with the patience of reception, performed with exact mercy. The Fripp reference could have become a comfortable shrine. Coniglio uses it as a living tool. The sustained guitar synth lines carry an unmistakable ancestry, and his Venetian sensibility bends the language toward silt, fog, industrial resonance, lagoon dusk and civic melancholy. Cosmic reach gains tidal pull; celestial shine gains mineral grain. It favors gradual pressure over flight. Its beauty comes from held attention, from discipline around ornament, from a faith in the long curve. In this sense, the album belongs to a lineage where technology gains dignity through restraint. Machines are allowed to sing because the hand guiding them has learned how to wait. The old dream of ambient music, sound as environment, gains a sharper contour here: this is ambient as causality, ambient as memory under voltage, ambient as the patient study of what follows an act. ~Mirco Salvadori The longer central movements hold the listener in a suspended physics. Coniglio’s delays behave like planets with fixed orbits, while his improvisational gestures act like sudden lights crossing those orbits. The album’s conceptual frame, hovering between classical causality and quantum possibility, could sound academic on paper. In practice it becomes deeply sensual. You hear destiny as overlap. You hear freedom as timing. You hear the smallest intervention opening a field of possible futures. The old dream of ambient music, sound as environment, gains a sharper contour here: this is ambient as causality, ambient as memory under voltage, ambient as the patient study of what follows an act. The mastering by James E Armstrong leaves the work broad and breathing, preserving the soft grain of the delays and the syruped density of the reverbs. James Osland’s artwork, pale, concrete toned, touched by spectral color, mirrors the music with striking precision: a muted surface crossed by hidden radiance. This visual restraint matters, because the album itself operates through muted force. It glows by accumulation. It does its most powerful work through recurrence, through patient returning, through an elegant distance from easy climax. By the time the final tones dissolve, 13/19/32 A Catalogue Of Delays has described an entire poetics of return. It speaks of how time copies us, how each act sends replicas into the hours ahead, how memory may be exact and still feel mysterious. Coniglio has made an album that honors the craft of earlier soundscape practice while carrying it into a private, contemporary meditation on cause, chance and presence. It is beautiful, grave, lucid, quietly overwhelming. A catalogue, yes, and a weather system of the mind: measured, human, radiant, and filled with the solemn grace of sounds that know where they came from and where they are going. 13/19/32 A Catalogue of Delays is available on Elm. [Bandcamp] 13/19/32 A Catalogue of Delays by Enrico ConiglioThe post Enrico Coniglio :: 13/19/32 A Catalogue of Delays (Elm) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

LoMo delivers to Neo Ouija an album capable of conversing with the ambient techno tradition and with the more introspective sensibility of IDM, sustained by writing that is lucid, visionary and deeply musical. Ambient techno, IDM, electro and acid dust search for a shared temperature 29526 by LoMo   Lorenzo Montanà reappears under the LoMo moniker with the awareness of an artist who has crossed the long currents of European electronic music, leaving behind a precious and recognizable trail, fed by vision and sonic rigor since the five chapters of Labyrinth shared with Pete Namlook, works in which synthesis became thought, inner geography, austere journey. 29526 is born from that active memory and carries it into a more porous present, where ambient techno, IDM, electro and acid dust search for a shared temperature. The album moves like an organism slowly coming to life. Its seven parts share the same skin, made of wide low frequencies, minute arpeggios, softened impulses and melodic vapors that filter through with discretion. Its form has the rare virtue of continuity. Each section seems to generate the next by transfusion, with the pulse surfacing, vanishing, returning in denser form, then giving itself over to extended harmonic fields. Montanà works through sedimentation, through molecular attraction. The sounds arrive from afar, take on color, shift density, open into regular spirals, then yield to a more rarefied light. Namlook’s presence runs through 29526 like a familiar code, a trace left in the way time expands, in the trust placed in long motion, in the preference for patient hypnosis. LoMo has a highly recognizable voice. The album possesses an almost tactile Italian grace, a care for detail that softens even its most technical side. The patterns ignite with laboratory precision, the chords carry a milky hue, the acid pulses slip in with elegance, like green veins inside transparent matter. The cover art captures this cellular idea with precision, a living nucleus enclosed in clear forms, synthetic botany, imagined biology, the science of dream. The music within 29526 calls for full attention, preferably through headphones, where the lateral micro currents become part of the narration. Beneath the calm surface, a meticulous work on planes is in motion. The basses draw a deep propulsion, the mid range sequences build elastic lines, the upper frequencies bring small reflections. The beauty of the album is born from this exact measure. LoMo chooses a writing that breathes, able to open images through pressure, echo and rotation. This is music that knows the club as a distant memory and transforms it into mental energy, a quiet march toward a more contemplative zone. Able to open images through pressure, echo and rotation :: 29526 lives inside a fascinating balance between discipline and abandon. The structures possess an almost classical clarity, the internal passages flow with naturalness, the layers seem moved by a biological necessity. At times the album brushes against the sleekest electro, with subtle rhythmic deviations and polished bass lines. Elsewhere it lets vast ambient suspensions emerge, crossed by dissolving glimmers. The IDM component reveals itself in the precision of the detail, in the way rhythmic particles are distributed across the sound field. The techno element acts as a submerged engine, a pulsing presence in the blood of the composition. There is a particular narrative quality, almost novelistic, in the way Montanà arranges matter and silence. 29526 tells of a navigation in which the past of European electronic music returns as a living grammar, with nostalgia transformed into formal impulse. The lesson of FAX, of cosmic voyages and long analog spans, is received with respect and then filtered through a contemporary sensibility, more liquid, more organic, more attentive to the nuances of perception. In this passage LoMo finds his own reason for being, bringing memory and invention, machine and landscape, rhythm and contemplation into close alignment. “In this passage LoMo finds his own reason for being, bringing memory and invention, machine and landscape, rhythm and contemplation into close alignment.” ~Mirco Salvadori The production confirms the hand of an author accustomed to thinking of sound as total matter. Everything feels calibrated, chiseled, immersed in enveloping depth. Reverberant tails stretch out like pale comets, the sequences move with patience, the acid resonances open small fluorescences within the harmonic fabric. The album grows through a slow accumulation of intensity. It enters quietly and works for a long time, with a discreet force, almost subterranean. In its flow one feels the wisdom of someone who has crossed many seasons of electronic music and now chooses the path of synthesis, elegant subtraction, and the detail that illuminates the whole. 29526 is a return under another name and, at the same time, a departure. LoMo delivers to Neo Ouija an album capable of conversing with the ambient techno tradition and with the more introspective sensibility of IDM, sustained by writing that is lucid, visionary and deeply musical. Its strength lies in the way it turns the number of its title into an enigma, into inner coordinates, into a sonic cipher pulsing between synthetic green and lunar brightness. Montanà signs a mature, coherent work rich in reflections, where the memory of Namlook becomes an impulse to continue, an energy that crosses time and keeps generating listening. 29526 is available on Neo Ouija. items.body: Rotostyles is a vertiginous and exhilarating demonstration of sonic craftsmanship, draped in colossal, almost Dantean orchestration. Highly recommended—uneasy and captivating in equal measure. A monolithic, lysergic drone sequence that progressively mutates Lotophagus Records is a continuously surprising and highly productive French label with a broad vision of experimental and challenging music, ranging from modern chamber post-rock and semi-electronic works to fully immersive explorations of advanced compositional technologies. This album is the result of a creative collaboration between two acclaimed French sound artists with solid backgrounds, whose work is highly appreciated by listeners devoted to sonic excursions and music that exists far beyond the mainstream and the ordinary. I first encountered the releases of Michel Madrange (alias M.Nomized) through his uncompromising, enigmatic, hypnotic, disembodied, and thrilling post-industrial recordings for Cold Spring and the now-defunct Europa Café. His musical signature reveals clear affinities with the singular, enduring, and alchemical sonic explorations of Mauro Teardo, Contraste, Nurse With Wound, and other iconoclastic names who have earned a lasting reputation within the understated musical underground. I discovered the work of Julien Ash more recently, notably through Lotophagus, thanks to his collaborative effort with Philippe Neau, reviewed on Igloo Magazine. On Rotostyles, the two sound artists distill their distinctive vision and forward-thinking, singular approach to musical orchestration and textural sound design. The album opens with a monolithic, lysergic drone sequence that progressively mutates into something more dynamic and animated. Throughout, it remains remarkably attentive to detail, movement, and unexpected microtonal events. The result is a brilliant, neuronal, and psychoactive sonic journey that opens the doors of perception. Its palette of sounds is in constant flux, driven by spacious motifs and the physicality of textures draped in a foreboding atmosphere. The tense and mysteriously haunting impact occasionally erupts into a maelstrom of grandiose atonality, at times recalling the contemporary dramaturgy of Penderecki, Roland Kayn, Stephen Thrower, or Ligeti, as heard in the massive “Stories of Hapoti.” All in all, Rotostyles is a vertiginous and exhilarating demonstration of sonic craftsmanship, draped in colossal, almost Dantean orchestration. Highly recommended—uneasy and captivating in equal measure. Rotostyles is available on Lotophagus. items.body: For anyone familiar with the Italian underground electronic scene, Diskonnekt may appear to be a relatively new name. In reality, the duo is the result of years of musical experience brought together in a project that finally allowed its members to fully embrace their passion for electronic music. The band was formed in 2018 by producer and composer Vincenzo together with vocalist Andrea. The name Diskonnekt carries a meaning that goes beyond its dancefloor-friendly sound: it symbolizes the need to disconnect from what has become harmful or no longer serves a purpose, and reflects a broader commentary on today’s digital world, where an early internet that was once open and unrestricted has gradually evolved into an environment dominated by control and regulation. With “La Morte Del Sole” released by Halotan Records, Diskonnekt now presents a new chapter in its artistic journey. The album further develops the duo’s dark electro sound, combining powerful rhythms with an introspective atmosphere. It provided the opportunity to talk with the band about the origins of Diskonnekt, the ideas that drive their music, and the creative process behind the new release. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Diskonnekt interview Q: “La Morte Del Sole” is your second album. How did the transition from your debut album to this new work unfold? What were the main triggers and sources of inspiration behind both the music and the lyrics? Vincenzo: The earliest songs of the first album were quite Experimental. At that time I preferred to make faster songs with D’n’B rhythms and hardstyle elements, while keeping the darkness in the melodies. All combined with Andrea’s screaming. It was all instinctive, I didn’t think about chasing any genre. I liked to have various bases from song to song cause I didn’t want to get bored myself listening to the songs first. Then I started to slow down a bit and came out something that we liked more and more, using more the pounding rhythm typical of Techno but also of EBM. This transition phase is represented by a 3-track EP released in 2021, as well as the single “Eyeopener”. We got a taste for it and in 2024, while I was going through a very controversial personal period, I started writing the songs contained in the new album. “La Morte Del Sole“ is the impossibility of reaching the truth, both in the knowledge of everyday events and in personal relationships. Some lyrics are a bit introspective and personal such as “Oggi Qualcosa Muore” (translated “Today Something Dies”), others talk about the reality that surrounds us in a decadent key. Some others express irrepressible impulses and strong feelings for which one can go so far as to die. The pounding and distorted rhythm typical of EBM comes to our aid as a solid basis for expressing our points of view, added with our beloved Acid parts, dark atmospheres and melodies. Q: How did “La Morte Del Sole” come to life? Could you take us through the different stages of its creation, from the initial ideas to the finished album? What were the greatest challenges you faced, and which moments gave you the strongest sense of accomplishment? Vincenzo: The first song that established the new formula was “Piombo (Lead)”. As I always do, I started from the rhythm. As a big fan of The Prodigy, the part I like to take care of the most is B’n’D, because it’s  the one that drag everything forward and make the floor shake. Choosing the sounds this time was a longer and more refined process, I never wanted to settle. It was a fairly long and delicate process, and not easy. Each track needs its time. I also took care of post-production much more, I personally took care of everything including mastering. Andrea’s voice in this new formula has found the right space to best express all the anger. The biggest challenge each time is to simplify everything, because often during the composition different sounds and layers are inserted which are then useless and even dispersive. Simplicity and being direct are the hardest things to obtain. But once finished, the album immediately gave us a great feeling. And we wish the same to our listeners. We can say we put on it everything we had inside. Q: One thing that immediately struck me while listening to the album is the constant sense of power and aggression that runs through the songs. It feels as though a great deal of anger, frustration, and tension found its way into the music. To what extent is music a means of channeling, regulating, or even exorcising such emotions? How do you personally experience this process, and what role does making music play in your life beyond artistic expression? Vincenzo: Music is literally my everything. I could not fulfill myself in anything else. In addition, I work in a music rehearsal room so I live every day in contact with bands. But as I live it, making music is above all catharsis. A process of personal purification, the final effect of which is a transfer of energy. In our case, as you well said, a considerable amount of power and aggression comes out. Because these are the sensations that, first of all as listeners, give us energy. Music is a form of non-verbal communication, but very strong and powerful, for us the most natural way of communicating our emotions. Q: Many Dark-Electro artists present a dystopian vision of the future, and Diskonnekt is no exception. Do you feel that reality has now overtaken fiction in that regard? Looking at the world today, how much do these developments affect you personally, both as artists and as human beings? Vincenzo: I think that we no longer need to think about a dystopian future, reality has now outclassed it. Living in a society where truth is almost a crime and lies are dogma, we have exceeded all expectations in this regard. Orwell’s “1984”  is no more science-fiction. Of course, all this is a source of inspiration, as we prefer to talk about the sick part of existence, both inside and outside of us. You can read it more or less explicitly in the lyrics. “Realtà A Circuito Chiuso” (translated: “Closed-Loop Reality”), for example, refers to the myth of Plato’s cave, of how one can get to see the truth and continue to prefer the lie, because perhaps more comfortable, to be socially accepted. “La Morte Del Sole” (translated “Death Of The Sun”) is the child of today’s reality, the perversion of power without limits, the celebration of lies, the truth (the sun) impossible to pursue, the overload. Q: I imagine that performing live is an essential aspect of Diskonnekt, especially given the importance of atmosphere and visual presentation within the genre. What have your experiences on stage been so far, and what do you hope to convey to an audience when you perform live? Is there a particular mission or philosophy behind your live shows? Andrea: We started performing live right away, even before we released the first songs. We have a great desire to broadcast our music live. Being two people on the stage, sometimes we made use of some dancers, some experiments turned out to be very relevant and we think we can repeat it in the future. Combined with the right atmosphere and the right audience, our musical proposal can be better appreciated on live performances. Often it happens that people who come to our concerts do not know us and discover us in this way, this makes us very happy. Our mission is to convey all our energy to people. Q: If you had to associate Diskonnekt with a film, a book, a historical event, a specific year, and another artist or band, what would you choose in each case, and why? Andrea: We could associate it with films like “The Matrix” or “Strange Days”, because Diskonnekt has that nocturnal atmosphere, a bit dystopian and melancholic, but with flashes of light. It’s music that makes you feel like you’re in a rainy city at 3 a.m., where everything seems disconnected but is actually connected. A real closed-circuit reality. About Diskonnekt Diskonnekt is an Italian dark electro duo formed in 2018 by producer and composer Vincenzo together with vocalist Andrea. The project released its self-titled debut album in 2020, followed in 2021 by a 3-track EP and the single “Eyeopener”. A further single, “Radio Otagron”, appeared in 2024. Diskonnekt’s second album, “La Morte Del Sole”, was released on 10 April 2026 through Halotan Records as a seven-track digipack CD and digital album, with free MP3 and FLAC downloads offered through the label. Side-Line reviewed the album on 14 June 2026, rating it 9 out of 10 and calling Diskonnekt “a name to remember”. This interview marks Diskonnekt’s first extended conversation with Side-Line, covering the origins of the project, the themes behind “La Morte Del Sole”, and how the band approaches its live shows.

items.body: PAHL!, the German electro-industrial art and music collective from Leipzig, released the digital single “Digital Oblivion” on May 15, 2026. The PAHL! “Digital Oblivion” single merges icy electro-industrial sounds with dark-pop elements and electronica, addressing the tension between digital life and human connection. Digital Oblivion by PAHL! PAHL!’s ‘Digital Oblivion’: themes and credits “Digital Oblivion” was written with music by PAHL! and lyrics by Leo von Leibnitz, and mastered by Neil Pickles at RevealSound in London. PAHL! describes the track as posing the question, “what remains of us when everything turns digital?”, and centers the song on the irreplaceable value of authentic relationships as daily life moves further online. The single is available to stream on Bandcamp and Spotify. About PAHL! PAHL! is a Leipzig-based electronic art and music collective founded in November 2014 by Olaf Parusel (also of sToa), Peter Hardlab and Leo von Leibnitz (who also records as Digital Factor, Y-Luk-O and Promo.Fabrik). The three musicians united after growing dissatisfied with their existing projects, holding their first joint studio session in January 2015. PAHL! issued the debut single “Telos” in September 2021 as the first taste of a forthcoming album. The debut album, “I”, followed on April 4, 2022, recorded by the trio with additional vocals from Viola Manigk. Later that year, PAHL! released the video “Smash the Hope“, a black-and-white reworking referencing Stanley Kubrick’s cinema and adapted to the 2022 political climate, and played its first live show on September 17, 2022, at Kunstkraftwerk in Leipzig, presenting an audiovisual set across 15 projection screens. The band describes its work as sitting between concert, cinema, philosophy and performance art, with “Digital Oblivion” continuing PAHL!’s focus on the effects of digital life on human relationships.

items.body: Swiss industrial metal trio UNMUT released the EP “Revolution from Within” on May 29, 2026 through Grom & Lord Records. The five-track EP was recorded in Zürich, Switzerland between 2024 and 2025 and mastered by KARK Studios in Ålesund, Norway. The release is available digitally through Bandcamp. UNMUT bring an industrial metal sound that mixes extreme metal weight with darkwave and dark ambient atmospheres across the EP’s five tracks: “Revolution from Within (Eternal Fall)”, “The Feed”, “Ghosts of Our Lives”, “Seraphic Silhouette” and “Das Grab Deckt Meine Furcht”. Revolution from Within by UNMUT UNMUT consists of Umbra (guitars, programming, vocals), Flegel (vocals, bass) and Ean Lord (vocals), with additional vocals by M.L. Artwork and layout for “Revolution from Within” are by Samuel Trümpy. An official video for “Seraphic Silhouette” is embedded below. About UNMUT UNMUT is a Swiss industrial metal trio consisting of Umbra, Flegel and Ean Lord. The band debuted in 2024 with the EP “Flesh-Imprisoned Spirit,” released on February 27, 2024 through Detriti Records on cassette (catalog DR130), combining an extreme metal foundation with early industrial aesthetics and darkwave atmospheres. That debut drew a review from I Die: You Die in July 2024, which described the EP as pairing funereal synths with a doom-leaning industrial metal core alongside second-wave goth rock and darkwave elements. UNMUT followed up with “Revolution from Within,” released May 29, 2026 through Grom & Lord Records, a one-person independent label run by Leandro S. Pacheco. The EP was recorded in Zürich between 2024 and 2025 and mastered by KARK Studios in Ålesund, Norway, continuing the band’s combination of industrial metal, gothic and darkwave atmospheres with extreme metal and dark ambient elements.

items.body: Timo Cromm—also known for his work with Reichsfeind—has been active under the name Destroy Me Again for several years. For “Fill The Void”, he selected no fewer than 18 tracks from the project’s back catalogue, reworking them into fresh new versions and even re-recording the vocals. Destroy Me Again remains instantly recognizable, staying true to its distinctive Future-Pop influences. There is a perfect balance between driving EBM basslines and soaring Trance-inspired leads, resulting in a sound that is powerful, melodic, and irresistibly danceable. At the same time, Destroy Me Again offers enough variety, making room for a few calmer, dreamier compositions alongside the more energetic material. There are darker moments as well, while several tracks are enhanced by beautiful male-female vocal duets. I hesitate to make direct comparisons, but fans of X Marks The Pedwalk will undoubtedly find plenty to appreciate here. Fill The Void is an excellent retrospective that not only highlights the evolution of Destroy Me Again but also demonstrates why this project deserves a much wider audience. (Rating:8). Listen to “Persona”: Persona by Destroy Me Again About Destroy Me Again Destroy Me Again is a project based in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, signed to Infacted Recordings. It is fronted by Timo Cromm, who is also known for his work with Reichsfeind. The project’s catalogue includes the albums “Living In Space”, “Dopamin” and “Cold By Design”, along with several earlier EPs. For “Fill The Void”, Cromm revisited 18 songs from that back catalogue, reworking the arrangements and re-recording the vocals for a retrospective set that spans the project’s Future-Pop sound.

items.body: 『シャーマニズム——古代的エクスタシー技術』(仏語原題:Le Chamanisme et les techniques archaïques de l'extase)は、ミルチャ・エリアーデによる、世界各地のシャーマニズムのさまざまな形態を扱った歴史学的研究書です。フランスのリブレリー・パイヨ社から1951年にフランス語で刊行されました。その後、翻訳者ウィラード・R・トラスクによって英訳され、プリンストン大学出版局(ボリンゲン・シリーズ)から1964年に刊行されました。 全648ページに及ぶ大著で、2004年版はプリンストン・クラシックスとしてペーパーバック化され、増補改訂版としてリリースされています。出典: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamanism:_Archaic_Techniques_of_Ecstasy / https://www.ebay.de/p/6032780■ 構成・目次本書は理論編(前半)と地域別記述編(後半)の二部構成になっています。前半の主要な章立てはおおよそ以下の通りです。第I章:シャーマニズムと神秘的召命——シャーマン資質を授かる3つのアプローチ(西・中央シベリアにおけるシャーマンの選出、ツングース族における選出、ブリヤート族・アルタイ族における選出、世襲による伝授と自ら求めることによる獲得、シャーマニズムと精神病理学)第II章:イニシエーションの病気と夢——病気=イニシエーション、ヤクート族シャーマンのイニシエーション的エクスタシーと幻視、サモエード族シャーマンのイニシエーション的な夢、ツングース族・ブリヤート族などにおけるイニシエーション、オーストラリアの呪術師のイニシエーション、南北アメリカ・アフリカ・インドネシアにおけるイニシエーション的な解体、エスキモー・シャーマンのイニシエーション、自らの骸骨を観想する行、部族のイニシエーションと秘密結社そして後半は地域ごとの記述に充てられており、中央・北アジア、南北アメリカ、東南アジアとオセアニア、チベット・中国・極東など、シャーマニズムが見られる世界各地の展開を扱っています。 さらに終盤には、インド・ヨーロッパ語族の中のシャーマン的イデオロギーと技術を扱う章(古代ゲルマン人におけるエクスタシー技術、古代ギリシア、スキタイ人・コーカサス人・イラン人、古代インドの上昇儀礼と飛翔、タパスとディークシャー、インド先住民族のシャーマニズム)や、太鼓・馬・犬などのシンボリズムを横断的に扱う比較神話の章が置かれています。出典: https://shanyomaelibrary.wordpress.com/2026/06/16/shamanism-archaic-techniques-of-ecstasy-by-mircea-eliade/ / https://thoughtsonpapyrus.com/2020/05/19/review-shamanism-archaic-techniques-of-ecstasy-by-mircea-eliade/■ 中心となる定義と理論本書全体を貫く出発点となる定義は、シャーマニズムをまず「エクスタシーの技術」として捉えることです。この複合的な現象についての第一の、そしておそらく最も無難な定義は「シャーマニズム=エクスタシーの技術」である、とエリアーデ自身が述べています。要するに、その本質に立ち返れば、シャーマニズムとは単にエクスタシーの技術に他ならず、そしてそのエクスタシーは人間精神そのものと同じくらい古いものだ、という立場です。エリアーデが挙げるシャーマン資格の必須要件としては、シャーマンとしての召命が一種の危機として現れること、シャーマン候補者が象徴的な死と復活を経験すること、そしてシャーマンが独自のトランス状態を専門とし、そのトランス中に魂が肉体を離れて天に昇る、あるいは冥界に降りると信じられていること、が挙げられます。またその技術はエクスタシー的でありながら高度に統制されたものであり、エクスタシーそれ自体が目的なのではなく、魂の旅の一部として位置づけられます。この点でエリアーデはシャーマニズムを、受動的な憑依やディオニュソス的狂乱とは明確に区別しました。シャーマニズムと関連しうる治療者・占い師・エクスタシー実践者は、ディオニュソスとは何の関係もない。ディオニュソス的な神秘の流れはまったく異なる構造を持っており、バッカス的な熱狂はシャーマン的エクスタシーとは似ていない、と述べています。シャーマンになる経路としては、自発的な召命(「呼びかけ」あるいは「選抜」)、世襲による伝授、そして自ら求めて修行するという三つの道があるとされます。 宇宙論的な枠組みとしては、シャーマン文化はおおむね「下界・中間世界・上界」という三層構造の宇宙を想定し、それらは宇宙軸あるいは世界樹(のちにエリアーデが1950年代に導入・普及させた「アクシス・ムンディ」という概念)によって結ばれている、とされます。 象徴面では、シャーマンの言語は動物の鳴き声に由来し、それは異界や天界と交信する能力に等しいとされ、精霊としての動物はシャーマンのもう一つの自己(アルターエゴ)になりうるとも論じられます。さらにエリアーデは、シャーマンが共同体において果たす社会的機能を重視し、シャーマンは共同体の精神的な統合を守るという本質的な役割を担ってきた、悪霊や病気だけでなく黒魔術師とも戦い、生・健康・豊穣・光の世界を、死・病・不毛・災厄・「闇」の世界から守るのだ、と位置づけています。出典: https://www.ipl.org/essay/Eliades-Shamanism-Archaic-Techniques-Of-Ecstasy-PCEW9HDU8SM / https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/28022.Shamanism / https://lightbeing.blog/2025/07/18/shamanism-and-the-architecture-of-religious-experience/ / https://graphsearch.epfl.ch/fr/concept/71905122 / https://graphsearch.epfl.ch/en/concept/1831837■ 「旧石器起源」仮説とパラレリズムへの批判本書後半で地域ごとの記述を積み重ねたうえで、エリアーデは、世界各地に見られるこれらのシャーマニズムはすべて、旧石器時代における人類最古の宗教という共通の起源を持っていたはずだと論じました。刊行当時、本書はシャーマニズムというテーマ全体を初めて包括的に扱い、同時にそれを宗教史全体の中に位置づけようとした先駆的・権威ある研究として評価されましたが、その後数十年をかけて人類学・歴史学の研究が進展・精緻化するにつれ、「シャーマニズム」という一つの語で呼びうる世界共通の現象が存在するという前提や、すべてのシャーマニズムが単一の共通起源を持つというエリアーデの主張そのものが、次第に精査・疑問視の対象となっていきました。出典: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamanism:_Archaic_Techniques_of_Ecstasy■ ジェンダーをめぐる指摘本書の記述には男性シャーマンを中心に据えた偏りがあるという指摘もあります。第2章にある「シャーマンになろうとする若い男性あるいは女性は、選ばれた師のもとに贈り物を持って赴く」という一文について、エリアーデがあえて「男性」を先に置いた語順そのものが、性別による優劣意識を表しているとする分析もあります。エリアーデの記述の中で女性シャーマンへの言及は少なく、それはおそらく彼の調査資料自体に女性シャーマンについての知見が乏しかったためではないか、シャーマン文化においては男性が主要かつ支配的な役割を担ってきたようだ、とする読解も見られます。同時に、それは女性がシャーマニズムに関与していなかったことを意味するわけではない、とも付言されています。出典: https://www.ipl.org/essay/Eliades-Shamanism-Archaic-Techniques-Of-Ecstasy-PCEW9HDU8SM■ 「シャーマニズムは精神疾患か」という論争本書はシャーマニズムと神経症・精神病理との関連についても論じており、この点は学界で繰り返し議論の的となってきました。批判者の中には、エリアーデの記述が天界への上昇的な体験を過度に重視する一方で、多くの先住民の実践に見られる冥界への旅の経験を軽視しており、こうした偏りがシャーマニズムの真正な伝統の理解を歪めかねない、と論じる者もいます。この立場からは、エリアーデの記述は歴史的文脈や客観性を欠いており、彼自身のキリスト教神秘主義的な傾向を反映したものであって、特定の部族の実践に即した記述というよりも一般化されたイニシエーション儀礼像になっている、彼の著作は正確な学術的シャーマニズム研究というよりもネオシャーマニストのための信仰書としての性格を帯びている、とまで批判されています。出典: https://www.academia.edu/40048872/Archaic_techniques_of_ecstasy学界内部からの方法論批判としては、イオアン・ペトル・クリアーヌやジョナサン・Z・スミス、ジョヴァンニ・カザディオといった宗教史家たちが、エリアーデの比較的アプローチの限界を指摘してきました。エリアーデはシャーマニズムを民族学的・社会学的・心理学的現象として明確に区別しつつ、聖と俗の間の弁証法的な視座こそが宗教史家に固有の視点だと位置づけ、宗教現象の深い意味を解読することは宗教史家の役割に他ならない、という自身の方法論をこの著作全体を通じて実践しました。出典: https://www.academia.edu/37875859/_Shamanism_in_North_Asia_as_a_religious_phenomenon_A_brief_note_on_Mircea_Eliade_s_morphology_■ 刊行当時の書評本書は刊行当初から高く評価され、書評では次のような評言が繰り返し引用されています。エリアーデは共感と距離感を巧みに併せ持った筆致でシャーマンたちについて書いている、その知見はやがて未来の偉大な声によって反響されるだろう、というニューヨーク・タイムズ・ブック・レビューの評、詳細かつ比較的な視座からシャーマニズムを扱ったこの研究はこの主題における標準的な著作となった、とするタイムズ・リテラリー・サプルメントの評、そしてこれまでに出版されたシャーマニズム研究の中で明らかに最良の著作である、とするレビュー・オブ・リリジョンの評などです。フランク・カーモード(ニュー・ステイツマン誌)は、エリアーデを現代の神話研究において最も情報量豊かな案内人と評しました。出典: https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691210667/shamanism / https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/shamanism-mircea-eliade/1116856571■ ネオシャーマニズム・ニューエイジへの影響という論点本書のもう一つの大きな側面は、学術的評価とは別に、1960年代以降の西欧における「ネオシャーマニズム(新シャーマニズム)」運動の思想的源流の一つとなったことです。ネオシャーマニズム的な運動の起源は20世紀後半、とりわけカウンターカルチャー運動やポストモダニズムに遡るとされ、シャーマニズムおよびネオシャーマニズムに関する思想の普及・拡散に特に寄与した3人の書き手として、ミルチャ・エリアーデ、カルロス・カスタネダ、マイケル・ハーナーの名がしばしば挙げられます。1951年、エリアーデは本書の刊行によってシャーマンという観念を広く一般化させ、シャーマニズムを、霊的世界への旅を決定的な特徴とする一種の普遍的・原初的宗教として描き出しました。同時に、この点こそが最も厳しい学術的批判にもさらされた部分でもあります。人類学者アリス・ベック・キホーらは、「シャーマニズム」という語はシベリアのツングース族が自称する場合以外には用いるべきではない、と論じ、エリアーデの研究を厳しく批判しました。 それでも本書は、その後カスタネダやハーナーによって発展させられていくネオシャーマニズムにとって欠くことのできない土台となりました。エリアーデの著作は学術界の内部では大きく批判され、いくぶん周縁的な存在と見なされていた一方、西欧におけるネオシャーマニズムの創始的な著者たち——とりわけ「コア・シャーマニズム」と呼ばれる心理療法的技法を開発したマイケル・ハーナー(1982年)——にとっては、決定的に重要な影響源となりました。エリアーデ、カスタネダ、ハーナーはそれぞれのやり方でシャーマン的実践を脱文脈化・普遍化し、それを宗教の起源や、西洋が失った神秘的合一と結びつけていった、と分析されています。こうしたネオシャーマニズムの潮流とエリアーデ自身の学術的立場を区別しようとする擁護的な見方もあります。宗教学者としてのエリアーデは、その直観と想像力を大いに働かせたために宗教学史上もっとも議論を呼ぶ学者の一人となったが、それでも彼は自らの記述に丹念に註を付し、自身が扱う各シャーマン的伝統の間の相違点も類似点と同様に書き記していた点は評価に値し、その学問は熱狂的な支持者たちが称えるほど単純なものでも、批判者たちがこき下ろすほど単純なものでもなかった、とする評価です。出典: items.body: Jazzwerkstatt Peitz has a special place in the history of jazz festivals in Germany. First held in the 1970s and lasting through the early 1980s in the former East Germany, and then reinvigorated in 2011, the festival has been been parts cutting-edge, politically-subversive and nostalgic. After a generational change at the helm, Marie Blobel, daughter of the festival creator Ulli Blobel, has been updating, tweaking and re-inventing the weekend-long event, and winning the Deutscher Jazzpreis 2026 for Festival of the Year along the way. The Free Jazz Blog will be heading there in a couple weeks and will tell you all about it. In the meantime, enjoy this choice clip of an improvisation workshop from last year featuring a stellar cast of uncompromising musicians, namely Frank Gratkowski on alto sax and flute, Lotte Anker on saxophone, Kazuhisa Uchihashi on guitar, Antonio Borghini on double bass and Toma Gouband on drums. Learn more about the festival here and on the Free Jazz Blog here . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
